::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.640", Sentence = "This model provided an excellent account of the covariance matrix reported by Fu and Wang (χ² = 0.89, DF = 2, p = 0.640, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.004, RMSEA = 0.000 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.059], SRMR = 0.006)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. info.title: Questionable mediated effect of physical activity on smartphone addiction: A comment on Fu and Wang (2026)

author.affiliation:
Department of Clinical Neuroscience
								
									Karolinska Institutet
									Stockholm
									Sweden

text.text: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Fu and Wang, I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking physical activity to decreased smartphone addiction.

I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article.

In this alternative account, self-reported physical activity, self-control, health-promoting lifestyle, and smartphone addiction are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation.
The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern.
Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives.
Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.
The study by Fu and Wang Fu and Wang (2026) examined data from 712 Chinese college students of which 44.1% were female.
text.formatted: The study by <ref type="bibr">Fu and Wang Fu and Wang (2026)</ref> examined data from 712 Chinese college students of which 44.1% were female.

text.text: Measures of self-rated physical activity, self-control, health-promoting lifestyle, and smartphone addiction were administered.

Based on a serial mediation analysis, Fu and Wang concluded that "physical activity was significantly and negatively associated with smartphone addiction tendency among university students, with selfcontrol and health-promoting lifestyle acting as sequential mediators" (p. 1) and, moreover, that "these findings suggest that interventions could integrate physical activity, self-control training, and health-promoting lifestyle education, with priority given to enhancing self-control to promote a healthpromoting lifestyle, which may in turn be associated with lower smartphone addiction tendency" (p. 1).
Fu and Wang's interpretation is one possible explanation of the observed data, but it is not the only one.
Correlational evidence generally cannot establish the causal ordering of psychological variables (Reichenbach, 1971).
text.formatted: Correlational evidence generally cannot establish the causal ordering of psychological variables <ref type="bibr">(Reichenbach, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Distinct causal models may generate identical covariance structures, preventing researchers from determining which explanation is correct based solely on observed associations.
Consequently, conclusions regarding mechanisms may be influenced as much by theoretical assumptions embedded within statistical models as by the empirical observations themselves.

The purpose of this commentary is to illustrate this point through the presentation of an alternative model that reproduces the reported relationships while leading to a different theoretical interpretation.
All analyses were performed in R 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).
text.formatted: All analyses were performed in R 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the lavaan package <ref type="bibr">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The covariance matrix reconstructed from the summary statistics reported by Fu and Wang, together with the analysis code, is available on GitHub at https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.07.M.
text.formatted: The covariance matrix reconstructed from the summary statistics reported by Fu and Wang, together with the analysis code, is available on GitHub at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.07.M">https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.07.M</ref>.

text.text: The proposed alternative model is displayed in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The proposed alternative model is displayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Instead of treating physical activity as the initiating variable in a causal chain ending in decreased smartphone addiction, the model specifies self-rated physical activity, self-control, healthpromoting lifestyle, and smartphone addiction as indicators of a common latent construct, core selfevaluation.
Core self-evaluation reflects a person's overall appraisal of their own competence, worth, and effectiveness (Judge et al., 2004; Extremera and Rey, 2018).
text.formatted: Core self-evaluation reflects a person's overall appraisal of their own competence, worth, and effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Judge et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Extremera and Rey, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Under this framework, individuals with more positive core self-evaluations would be expected to report higher levels of physical activity, self-control, and health-promoting lifestyle and lower levels of smartphone addiction.
This model provided an excellent account of the covariance matrix reported by Fu and Wang (χ² = 0.89, DF = 2, p = 0.640, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.004, RMSEA = 0.000 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.059], SRMR = 0.006).
The theoretical implications of this model differ substantially from those suggested in the original article.
Fu and Wang interpreted their results as an indication that physical activity contributes to decreased smartphone addiction through the . . . .
1 intermediary roles of self-control and healthpromoting lifestyle.
By contrast, the latent-variable model treats all four observed variables as manifestations of an underlying disposition.
Because both models reproduce the same covariance structure, the mediation effects highlighted by Fu and Wang cannot be regarded as uniquely supported by the data.
Rather, they may reflect choices made during model specification rather than conclusions compelled by the empirical evidence.
The present reanalysis shows that the associations reported by Fu and Wang can be accommodated by more than one theoretically coherent explanation.

Whereas the original article emphasized a sequential process in which physical activity influences decreased smartphone addiction through self-control and health-promoting lifestyle, the alternative latent-variable model explains the same pattern of correlations without assigning a causal precedence to physical activity.
The aim of this commentary is not to argue that the original model is necessarily wrong.
Likewise, the good fit of the alternative model does not establish its correctness.
Rather, the key observation is that competing theoretical perspectives may account for the same set of empirical relationships.
When this occurs, statistical fit alone cannot identify the model that most accurately reflects the underlying psychological processes.
This limitation is particularly relevant for mediation analyses based on observational data.
Indirect effects are often interpreted as evidence of specific underlying mechanisms, yet cross-sectional and nonexperimental designs provide only limited information regarding causal direction.

When distinct models with contrasting theoretical implications fit the data well, conclusions regarding mechanisms, intervention priorities, and influencing pathways inevitably rest on assumptions that have not been directly tested.
For this reason, mediation results derived from observational datasets should be interpreted as tentative and conditional rather than as conclusive evidence of particular influencing processes.
This commentary is the latest in a series of critical evaluations of mediation analyses published in Frontiers in Psychology.
These commentaries have been submitted to Frontiers but have so far never been accepted for publication or even sent to review (Table 1).
